title: Polymorphism and Abstraction
goal: Call the right override through a base pointer, design abstract interfaces and avoid object slicing.

topics.title: virtual enables dynamic dispatch
topics.body: A virtual function is chosen by the object's dynamic type, not the pointer's static type. `override` makes a signature mismatch a compile error instead of a silent new function.

topics.title: Pure virtual makes an interface
topics.body: `= 0` makes the function pure virtual, so the class cannot be instantiated and every concrete derived class must implement it.

topics.title: Object slicing loses the derived part
topics.body: Copying a derived object into a base value slices off the derived fields, so the virtual call uses the base version. Pass by reference or pointer instead.

debug.title: Instantiating an abstract class
debug.error: error: cannot declare variable ‘s’ to be of abstract type ‘Shape’

debug.title: An override with the wrong signature
debug.error: Wrong output: 1 — the missing const made a different function, so the base version was called.

tasks.title: Shape area through a base reference
tasks.statement: Create a Shape base with a pure virtual area(), implement Square and print the area through a const Shape reference.

interviewBank.q: Why does a polymorphic base need a virtual destructor?
interviewBank.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs only the base destructor when it is not virtual, so the derived part is never destroyed. That is undefined behaviour and typically leaks.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
interviewBank.answer: Overloading picks a function by argument types at compile time within one scope. Overriding replaces a virtual function in a derived class and is selected at runtime by the object's type.

defenseBank.q: How would you explain polymorphism to a beginner?
defenseBank.answer: One instruction, many behaviours: calling area() on a shape works whether it is a square or a circle, and each type answers in its own way.
steps: Show that the caller did not change.

defenseBank.q: When is runtime polymorphism the wrong tool?
defenseBank.answer: When the type is known at compile time or the hot path cannot afford an indirect call. Templates or plain overloads resolve earlier and inline better.

title: Operator Overloading and Conversions
goal: Give a value type natural operators with correct semantics, and keep conversions explicit.

topics.title: A value type with operator+
topics.body: Return a new value, take the operands by const reference, and keep the operator const so it works on const objects.

topics.title: operator<< makes a type printable
topics.body: Stream insertion must be a non-member taking `std::ostream&` first. Returning the stream lets calls chain.

topics.title: Compound assignment returns the object
topics.body: `operator+=` modifies the left operand and returns `*this` by reference. `operator+` is then written once in terms of it, so the two cannot disagree.

debug.title: A stream operator that returns void
debug.error: error: invalid operands of types ‘void’ and ‘const char [2]’ to binary ‘operator<<’

debug.title: operator+ that mutates the left operand
debug.error: Wrong output: 7 7 — operator+ changed a, so the addition was not a pure operation.

tasks.title: Complex addition
tasks.statement: Implement Complex with operator+ and print the real and imaginary parts of (1,2) + (3,4).

interviewBank.answer: Stream insertion and extraction, and any operator whose left operand is not your type, such as `int + Complex`. They can be friends when they need private access.
`a = a` would otherwise free a resource before reading from it. The usual guard checks for `this == &other` before releasing anything.

defenseBank.q: Why is overloading `&&` or `,` usually a mistake?
defenseBank.answer: Both have built-in sequencing and short-circuit behaviour that a user-defined overload cannot reproduce, so code that relies on them silently changes meaning.
steps: Keep the operator for types where it is unsurprising.

defenseBank.q: What makes an operator overload defensible?
defenseBank.answer: It behaves like the built-in operator for that concept, has the expected return type and does not surprise with side effects. If a reader has to check the header, it probably should have been a named function.

title: Templates and Generic Programming
goal: Write one function or class that works for many types, and read template errors without panic.

topics.title: A function template
topics.body: The compiler generates a concrete function for each type used, so the same body works for int and double without runtime cost.

topics.title: A class template
topics.body: A class template parameterises the element type. Member functions defined outside the class need the template header and the qualified name.

topics.title: Two parameters, one algorithm
topics.body: Templates can take several parameters. The compiler deduces each from the arguments, and a mismatch between them is reported at the call site.

debug.title: Two different types for one T
debug.error: error: no matching function for call to ‘maximum(int, double)’

debug.title: A dependent type without typename
debug.error: error: need ‘typename’ before ‘T::size_type’ because ‘T’ is a dependent scope

tasks.title: Generic maximum
tasks.statement: Write a function template maximum<T> and print the larger of 3 and 7.

interviewBank.answer: It is the compiler generating a concrete function or class for the types actually used. Nothing is generated for types you never instantiate, which is why template errors often appear at the call site.

interviewBank.q: Why do template errors look so long?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler reports the full instantiation chain from your call down into the library. The useful line is usually the first note that names your type and the requirement that failed.

defenseBank.answer: When only one type is ever used, or when the abstraction forces every caller into the same algorithm. A plain function or a small interface is easier to read and debug.
steps: Check whether the types share the required operations.
Prefer the simpler non-template version when they do not.

defenseBank.q: What does it mean that templates are header-only in practice?
defenseBank.answer: The compiler needs the full definition to instantiate, so the body usually lives in the header. Putting it in a .cpp leaves other translation units unable to generate the code.

title: STL Containers
goal: Choose the right container for the access pattern and use vector, map and set without fighting their interfaces.

topics.title: vector is the default sequence
topics.body: `std::vector` stores its elements contiguously and grows geometrically, so push_back is amortised constant time and iteration is cache-friendly.

topics.title: map keeps keys sorted
topics.body: `std::map` is a balanced tree: lookup is logarithmic and iteration is in key order. `operator[]` inserts a default value when the key is missing, which is sometimes what you want and sometimes a bug.

topics.title: set stores unique keys
topics.body: A `set` removes duplicates and keeps order, so it is the tool for distinct values and membership tests rather than counts.

debug.title: operator[] on a const map
debug.error: error: passing ‘const std::map<int, int>’ as ‘this’ argument discards qualifiers [-fpermissive]

debug.title: at() past the end of a vector
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'

tasks.title: Count words with a map
tasks.statement: Count how often each word appears in the array {"a","b","a"} and print the count for "a".

interviewBank.q: vector, list or deque: how do you choose?
interviewBank.answer: Default to vector for contiguous storage and cache locality. Use deque when you need fast insertion at both ends, and list only when stable iterators and frequent middle insertion outweigh the pointer overhead.

map when order matters or you need range queries, unordered_map when average constant lookup matters more and the key can be hashed. The unordered version trades ordering and worst-case guarantees for speed.

defenseBank.q: Why does `map::operator[]` sometimes create a bug?
defenseBank.answer: It inserts a default-constructed value for a missing key, so a lookup that was meant to be read-only silently grows the container and changes later results.
steps: Use find or at when absence must be explicit.

defenseBank.q: How do you decide between a set and a vector for distinct values?
defenseBank.answer: If you need membership checks and ordering, a set gives both. If you only need uniqueness once, sort and unique a vector, which has better locality and a cheaper constant factor.

title: Iterators, Algorithms and Lambdas
goal: Replace hand-written loops with algorithms, pass behaviour as a lambda, and understand iterator invalidation.

topics.title: Algorithms take iterator ranges
topics.body: `std::sort` receives a begin and an end iterator, so it works on any contiguous or random-access range. Half-open ranges mean the end is one past the last element.

topics.title: A lambda is a local function object
topics.body: `[](int x) { return x > 2; }` is an anonymous callable. Captures bring in local state; `[&]` captures by reference and `[=]` by value.

topics.title: accumulate folds a range
topics.body: `std::accumulate` combines the elements with an initial value. The initial value's type is the result type, so `0.0` is needed for a double mean.

debug.title: sort called without its parentheses
debug.error: error: no matching function for call to ‘sort(std::vector<int>::iterator, <unresolved overloaded function type>)’

debug.title: erase-remove without the erase
debug.error: Wrong output: 3 — remove only shifts the kept elements; the container size changes only when erase runs.

tasks.title: Sort descending and sum
tasks.statement: Sort {1,3,2} descending with a lambda and print the first element and the total.

interviewBank.q: Why is erase(remove(...)) a two-step operation?
interviewBank.answer: remove_if moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end, but it cannot change the container's size because it only sees iterators. erase then removes the tail, which is why both calls are required.
Any reallocation, and any insertion or erase at or before the iterator's position. Reallocation happens on growth, so a stored iterator can dangle after a push_back even if no element was erased.

defenseBank.q: When is a hand-written loop clearer than an algorithm?
defenseBank.answer: When the loop performs several different actions in one pass, or the algorithm would need a lambda so complex that the loop is shorter. Algorithms win when they name a single operation.
steps: Name the single operation the loop performs.
Check whether an algorithm states it directly.
Keep the loop when the body does more than one thing.

defenseBank.q: Why do lambdas capture by reference carefully?
defenseBank.answer: A reference capture keeps a pointer to a local that may be gone when the lambda is called later, which is a dangling reference. Capture by value when the lambda outlives the scope.

title: Exception Handling and Error Management
goal: Signal failure with exceptions, catch them at the right level, and keep objects consistent while unwinding.

topics.title: throw, try, catch
topics.body: `throw` transfers control to the nearest matching `catch`. Stack objects are destroyed on the way out, which is what makes RAII the partner of exceptions.

topics.title: A custom exception type
topics.body: Derive from `std::runtime_error` when callers may want to catch a category. The `what()` message should say what failed, not just that something failed.

topics.title: noexcept is a promise
topics.body: `noexcept` states that a function will not throw. If it does, the program terminates, so mark only operations that genuinely cannot fail or must not.

debug.title: An exception nobody catches
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'

debug.title: Catching a polymorphic exception by value
debug.error: Wrong output: std::exception — catching by value slices the runtime_error, so the derived message is lost.

tasks.title: Safe divide
tasks.statement: Write divide that throws std::invalid_argument on zero, catch it and print the message.

interviewBank.q: When should you return an error code instead of throwing?
interviewBank.answer: When failure is expected and cheap to handle at every call site, or when the code is compiled without exceptions. Exceptions fit exceptional failures that cannot be handled locally.
That an operation leaves the program in a valid state when it throws: no leaks, no half-updated invariants. The strong guarantee adds that the operation either fully succeeds or changes nothing.

defenseBank.answer: A reference preserves the dynamic type for the handler and avoids a copy; const states that the handler does not modify the exception. Catching by value slices a derived exception.
steps: Show what the sliced copy loses.
Write the catch clause with const&.

defenseBank.q: Why not use exceptions for ordinary control flow?
defenseBank.answer: Throwing is expensive compared to a return, and it hides control flow from a reader. A loop that exits by exception is harder to reason about than one with a condition.
